newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel on suicide attack alert.
newsitem.headline: Israel on suicide attack alert.

text.p: Paramilitary police patrolled shopping malls and roadblocks snarled traffic on highways as Israel went on high alert on Sunday against a feared suicide attack by Islamic Jihad militants.

Israeli Army Radio said security forces had received new information a guerrilla squad was already in the Jewish state to avenge the October 26, 1995 assassination in Malta of Islamic Jihad leader Fathi Shqaqi.
Public Security Minister Avigdor Kahalani said the expected target was in one of the Israeli cities -- Jerusalem, Tel Aviv or Haifa.
"As far as we know there is a certain force, with defined goals, that is more less apparently in our territory," Kahalani told the radio.

"Security forces take this threat very seriously and so this preparedness," National Police Chief Assaf Hefetz said. "We don't know the kind of attack exactly but it could be an explosion, suicide, shots."
Roadblocks on the Jerusalem-Tel Aviv highway caused commuters hours of delays. The manager of Jerusalem's central bus station said the checkpoints prompted many would-be travellers to stay home.
At Jerusalem's main shopping mall, border police inspected cars. A sniffer dog was used to search for explosives. Large paramilitary forces patrolled the mall itself.
Israel's Industrialists Association said the security measures were hurting the economy.

"The increasing jitters are causing serious and significant economic damage. A morning like today causes a situation in which people don't want to go out shopping," said Yehoshua Abramovitch, a spokesman for the association.

Haim Ramon, a leader of Israel's main opposition Labour party, accused the right-wing government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of "causing general paralysis and putting the entire population into unnecessary hysterics and panic."
Islamic Jihad, responsible for suicide attacks in Israel, accuses the Jewish state of killing Shqaqi. His assassins were never caught.
Netanyahu told reporters that guerrillas were trying to torpedo Israel's peace moves with the Palestinians and said "external elements", which he did not name, were behind the planned attack.
Palestinian police in the Gaza Strip last month arrested dozens of Islamic Jihad members to pre-empt any attacks by the movement, a PLO security official said.

Islamic Jihad and Hamas leaders have been in jail since suicide bombings in February and March, responsibility for which was claimed by Hamas, the other leading Islamic resistance group in Palestinian areas.
Israel on October 23 sealed off the West Bank and Gaza Strip, barring Palestinians from going to work in the Jewish state, for fear of attacks. That closure remains in place.
British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind, on a one-day Middle East trip that included a visit to the West Bank town of Hebron and the Gaza Strip, called Jewish settlements illegal.
"The British government believes all Jewish settlements in the occupied territories are illegal and that they should not continue," he told reporters in Hebron.
Under an interim peace deal, Hebron was to be handed over to the PLO in March, but the move was delayed for security reasons.
The PLO and Israel have failed to reach agreement on the handover of the city, a flashpoint of violence where 400 settlers live and study among more than 100,000 Palestinians.

Trying to nudge Israel and the PLO closer to a deal, Rifkind said: "I think Hebron has become crucial to whether there is a future for the peace process...Without Hebron, it is rhetoric. With Hebron, it begins to look for real."
In Amman, Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov called for resumption of comprehensive Middle East peace talks.
"There is a need to have talks on all tracks at one time," Primakov told a news conference at the end of a week-long Middle East tour.
"Whatever achievement is made on one track, it could regress if there isn't progress on the others," he said, speaking through an interpreter.
Primakov said his trip, which took him to Syria, Lebanon, Israel, Egypt, the Palestinian territories and Jordan, had focused on defusing tension between Israel and Syria.
